title: Person Recognition at Altitude and Range: Fusion of Face, Body Shape and Gait

AI.tldr: The paper presents FarSight, an end-to-end system for whole-body person recognition at long range that fuses face, gait and body shape cues, and reports large gains over the authors' preliminary system on the BRIAR benchmark.
AI.motivation: Biometric recognition in surveillance is hard when data is captured at long standoff distances, high elevation angles and under turbulence or wind, which degrades images and causes pose, scale and cross-domain gaps.
AI.method: FarSight combines four modules: multi-subject detection and tracking, recognition-aware video restoration, modality-specific biometric feature encoding for face, gait and body shape, and quality-guided multi-modal fusion.
AI.result: Compared with the preliminary system, FarSight achieves a 34.1% absolute gain in 1:1 verification accuracy (TAR@0.1% FAR), a 17.8% increase in closed-set identification (Rank-20) and a 34.3% reduction in open-set identification errors (FNIR@1% FPIR) on the BRIAR dataset; it was also evaluated in the 2025 NIST RTE Face in Video Evaluation (FIVE).
AI.conclusion: The authors position FarSight as a state-of-the-art solution for operational biometric recognition in challenging real-world conditions.

title: GenHOI: Generalizing Text-driven 4D Human-Object Interaction Synthesis for Unseen Objects

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GenHOI, a two-stage framework that synthesises text-driven 4D human-object interaction sequences for objects unseen in training, reaching state-of-the-art results on OMOMO and 3D-FUTURE.
AI.motivation: Text-driven 4D human-object interaction synthesis lags behind human motion synthesis because large-scale 4D HOI datasets are scarce, and existing methods do not generalise well to unseen objects.
AI.method: The first stage uses an Object-AnchorNet, trained only on 3D HOI datasets, to reconstruct sparse 3D HOI keyframes for unseen objects. The second stage uses a Contact-Aware Diffusion Model (ContactDM) with a Contact-Aware Encoder to extract human-object contact patterns and Contact-Aware HOI Attention to inject contact signals, interpolating the keyframes into dense, temporally coherent 4D sequences.
AI.result: The abstract reports state-of-the-art results on the public OMOMO and 3D-FUTURE datasets and strong generalisation to unseen objects, with high-fidelity 4D HOI generation; no specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: GenHOI reduces dependence on large-scale 4D HOI data and generalises to unseen objects, which the authors present as a step toward high-fidelity 4D HOI synthesis.

title: Consecutive Preferential Bayesian Optimization

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Consecutive Preferential Bayesian Optimization (CPBO), which reuses the previous candidate in each pairwise comparison to cut production cost and models oracle indifference with a Just-Noticeable Difference threshold.
AI.motivation: Existing preferential Bayesian optimization ignores the cost of producing candidate solutions for evaluation, and it does not model the perceptual ambiguity of human feedback, which can be indifferent to small utility differences.
AI.method: CPBO uses a consecutive comparison setting in which each new candidate is compared against the previous one. It adds a Just-Noticeable Difference threshold to a probabilistic preference model and adapts an information-theoretic acquisition strategy that selects configurations most informative about the unknown optimum.
AI.result: The method shows a notable increase in accuracy in setups with high production costs or indifference feedback, and its practical feasibility is demonstrated on a real-world food extrusion task.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for production cost and perceptual ambiguity makes preferential optimisation more practical when candidates are expensive to produce or when human feedback is indifferent.

title: Why Is Dyck$_1$ Hard for Language Models? Learning and Generalizing a One-Counter Language.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how RNNs and Transformers learn and generalise the one-counter language Dyck-1 (balanced parentheses), finding strong depth and length generalisation despite formal expressivity limits, and identifying numerical sensitivity and length-by-range-of-dependence regions as predictors of failure.
AI.motivation: Formal proofs that RNNs and Transformers cannot recognise Dyck-1 rely on assumptions that do not carry over to practical settings, leaving a gap between theory and practice.
AI.method: The authors give a taxonomy of the assumptions behind theoretical and empirical claims and run controlled comparative experiments on learnability and generalisation in RNNs and Transformers with seven positional encodings.
AI.result: Both RNNs and Transformers show strong depth and length generalisation despite their formal inability to recognise Dyck-1 with unbounded precision; numerical sensitivity and jointly defined regions of length and range-of-dependence are identified as additional predictors of generalisation failure.
AI.conclusion: Human intuition may be a poor guide to what is algorithmically or mechanistically hard for neural networks.

title: FreeDeshadow: Shadow Removal for User-Specified Objects With Multimodal Prompts
summary: Existing shadow removal methods either perform global shadow removal or rely on precise shadow masks to guide restoration. Such paradigms limit their ability to selectively remove the shadow cast by a user-specified object in practical applications. To this end, we introduce an object-aware controllable shadow removal task, which allows users to specify a target object through a simple prompt and removes only its cast shadow while preserving other content. However, object-shadow asymmetry makes it challenging to establish accurate correspondence between the specified object and its spatially separated cast shadow and to confine restoration to the target shadow region. To address these challenges, we propose FreeDeshadow, a unified controllable shadow removal framework that supports both visual and textual prompts. It consists of an object-aware generator and a shadow-aware local refiner. The former interprets the user prompt and produces a high-quality shadow-free proposal, while the latter establishes the correspondence between the object and its cast shadow and constrains the generated changes to the target shadow region. To support training and evaluation, we further construct PCSRD+, a large-scale dataset containing 154,571 quadruples at 1024$\times$1024 resolution and covering six types of user prompts. The visual prompts include a dot, a line, and an object mask, while the textual prompts describe the target object using attributes, spatial relations, or states. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FreeDeshadow accurately removes the shadow of the target object under both visual and textual prompts while effectively preserving non-target regions. It also outperforms existing methods in shadow removal performance and controllability. Project Page: this https URL

AI.tldr: FreeDeshadow removes only the cast shadow of a user-specified object, guided by a visual or textual prompt, and leaves other content unchanged. The authors also release PCSRD+, a dataset of 154,571 quadruples at 1024x1024 resolution.
AI.motivation: Existing shadow removal is either global or needs precise shadow masks, so it cannot selectively remove the shadow of one object. Object-shadow asymmetry (the object and its cast shadow are spatially separated) makes correspondence and confinement of the edit hard.
AI.method: A unified framework with an object-aware generator that interprets the prompt and produces a shadow-free proposal, and a shadow-aware local refiner that links the object to its cast shadow and limits changes to the target shadow region. Supports visual prompts (dot, line, object mask) and textual prompts (attributes, spatial relations, states).
AI.result: The method removes the target object's shadow under both visual and textual prompts while preserving non-target regions, and outperforms existing methods in shadow removal quality and controllability. Evaluated on PCSRD+ with six prompt types.
AI.conclusion: Object-aware, prompt-controllable shadow removal is practical and can be trained and evaluated at scale with the released dataset.

title: Fast Slice-Wise Deep Learning Motion Correction for Spinal Cord Functional MRI
summary: Respiratory and bulk motion displace the spinal cord between the volumes of a functional MRI time series. Current methods such as the Spinal Cord Toolbox (SCT) take several minutes per time series, and general-purpose brain tools register whole volumes, whereas the cord moves mainly slice by slice. We propose a lightweight convolutional neural network that regresses the in-plane translation aligning each axial slice to a reference. Two models, trained without motion labels, correct large and then residual motion. On a 3T (120 scans) and a 7T (59 scans) dataset, the proposed method improves on SCT on every metric (tSNR +10 to +25%, DVARS -20 to -38%), leaves almost no slice displaced by more than one voxel (<0.1%), performs on par with a slice-wise AFNI variant and better than slice-wise FSL FLIRT, and runs in about 10 s per scan, about 30 times faster than SCT. The code is available at this https URL and the method is available in SCT v7.4.

AI.tldr: A lightweight slice-wise CNN corrects in-plane motion of spinal cord fMRI by regressing a per-slice translation to a reference, trained without motion labels. It improves on Spinal Cord Toolbox (SCT) on all reported metrics and runs about 30 times faster.
AI.motivation: Spinal cord motion between fMRI volumes is mainly slice-by-slice, while SCT takes minutes per series and general brain tools register whole volumes.
AI.method: A CNN regresses the in-plane translation aligning each axial slice to a reference. Two models, trained without motion labels, correct large motion first and then residual motion.
AI.result: On 3T (120 scans) and 7T (59 scans) data, tSNR improves by 10 to 25 percent and DVARS decreases by 20 to 38 percent relative to SCT. Under 0.1 percent of slices are displaced by more than one voxel. It matches a slice-wise AFNI variant, beats slice-wise FSL FLIRT, and runs in about 10 s per scan, about 30 times faster than SCT.
AI.conclusion: Slice-wise learned motion correction is a fast, accurate alternative for spinal cord fMRI, and the method is available in SCT v7.4.

title: What Entropy-Based View Selection Cannot See: An Audit of Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Models
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshops on VLM4RWD
summary: Vision-language models such as CLIP can classify images into categories they were never explicitly trained to recognize, but accuracy degrades when test images differ in style or source from their training data. A common remedy generates randomly cropped and flipped copies of each test image, called views, and combines their predictions. Since some views miss the object, methods must identify which views to trust. The dominant approach uses prediction entropy to measure confidence and retains the most certain views. Other methods use signals such as embedding typicality. Despite repeated refinements of these scoring functions, the information they rely on, the model's own response to each view, remains largely unexamined. We investigate this choice while holding other pipeline stages fixed. First, we show that view selection, rather than the gradient update, accounts for almost all accuracy gains. We then examine whether entropy identifies useful views when predictions are wrong, despite at least one view predicting the correct class. In these cases, entropy ranks correct views above incorrect ones no better than chance, recovering only about one-twentieth of the accuracy recovered by an oracle over the same views. This finding holds across two image encoders and under a control ruling out an obvious statistical artifact. An exact analysis explains this limitation: entropy measures confidence but not which class a view favors. We identify an unused signal already available in the augmentation pipeline: the fraction of the original image retained by each crop. Ranking views by this quantity improves accuracy on 14 of 15 benchmark datasets over entropy and on 11 of 15 over the strongest scoring function tested. A pre-method measurement also predicts which datasets benefit.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that entropy-based view selection in test-time adaptation for CLIP fails to identify correct views, and that ranking views by the fraction of the original image retained by each crop improves accuracy on most benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Test-time augmentation methods for vision-language models rely on prediction entropy to pick confident views, but the information that drives this choice has not been examined.
AI.method: With other pipeline stages held fixed, the authors compare view selection against the gradient update, analyze entropy's ranking of correct versus incorrect views, run an exact analysis, and rank views by crop retained-area fraction, a signal already in the augmentation pipeline.
AI.result: View selection accounts for almost all accuracy gains. When some views are correct, entropy ranks them no better than chance, recovering about one-twentieth of the oracle's accuracy, across two encoders and under a control. Retained-fraction ranking improves accuracy on 14 of 15 datasets over entropy and on 11 of 15 over the strongest tested scoring function.
AI.conclusion: Entropy measures confidence but not which class a view favors, so view scoring should use other signals; a pre-method measurement also predicts which datasets benefit.

title: SyntheIce: A Synthetic Radargram Annotation Benchmark for Englacial Layer Reconstruction
comment: 10 pages, 10 figures, 3 Tables, accepted in IEEE International Conference on Big Data (BigData) 2026
summary: Englacial layers in radio-echo-sounding radargrams (subsurface ice images) encode the climate and flow history of ice sheets and glaciers. However, large-scale extraction is hindered by time-consuming manual annotation and semi-automated detectors that produce fragmented rather than continuous horizons. We address two challenges: reconstructing complete layers from partial detections across radargram profiles and validating layer continuity across adjacent tile boundaries. We introduce a slope-aware greedy fragment-linking algorithm that reconstructs full-width layers using row-similarity gating and an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) slope predictor. Each reconstruction receives a content-based hash ID for stable cross-radargram identification. For quantitative evaluation, we generate SyntheIce, a synthetic dataset of 600 radargrams spanning multiple complexity levels and realistic noise conditions, including 150 wide radargrams divided into four adjacent tiles. All samples include exact ground-truth annotations. We evaluate the dataset using XCheck, a consistency-based validation framework, extending its original two-image setting to four consecutive tiles and enforcing continuity at every boundary. This demonstrates the dataset's utility for developing and evaluating real-world annotation algorithms. Our findings extend beyond ice science: when spatial features are fragmented but retain consistent local geometry, trajectory-based linking is more reliable than appearance-based matching. Evaluation against expert-labeled real radargrams demonstrates high precision, recall, F1-score, and mean IoU, supporting the method's transfer to real-world data.

AI.tldr: SyntheIce provides a synthetic radargram benchmark of 600 radargrams for englacial layer reconstruction, together with a slope-aware greedy fragment-linking algorithm and an extension of the XCheck consistency framework to four tiles.
AI.motivation: Manual annotation of englacial layers is slow, and semi-automated detectors give fragmented horizons rather than continuous ones. Layer continuity across tile boundaries also needs validation.
AI.method: A greedy fragment-linking algorithm uses row-similarity gating and an EWMA slope predictor, with content-based hash IDs for reconstructions. XCheck is extended from two images to four consecutive tiles, enforcing continuity at each boundary.
AI.result: The synthetic dataset covers multiple complexity levels and noise conditions, with 150 wide radargrams split into four tiles, and includes exact ground truth. Evaluation on expert-labeled real radargrams reports high precision, recall, F1-score and mean IoU.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-based linking is more reliable than appearance-based matching when fragments keep consistent local geometry, and the method is expected to transfer to real data.

authors: Mario Alberto Tapia de la Cruz
title: RECALL: Real-Time Recalibration of Multi-Camera Rigs via Learned OEM-Anchored Residuals
summary: Multi-camera rigs ship pre-calibrated from the manufacturer, but their calibration goes stale each time the rig is repositioned, and drifts continuously through wear, thermal cycling, and vibration. Recovering it on-the-fly is hard: classical bundle adjustment needs a fresh multi-view capture and a global optimization whose cost grows with the rig, ruling out real-time use. In this paper we present RECALL, a feed-forward method that recalibrates a movable multi-camera rig in a single pass. From the nominal OEM calibration as an anchor and a brief observation of a known object, it predicts each camera's current intrinsics and extrinsics, written as a shared global rotation of the rig composed with a small per-camera drift. Instead of regressing the calibration in one shot, RECALL refines its estimate with a learned, rig-coupled recurrent operator that reprojects through a differentiable projection and applies attention across the cameras at each step, and solves for the shared rotational gauge in-network with a learned Gauss-Newton step rather than regressing it. Because the ground truth is synthesizable, we train entirely on data generated on-the-fly and need no captured dataset. On a synthetic 10-camera benchmark, RECALL is more accurate than per-camera and rig-coupled joint bundle adjustment ($0.26^\circ$ vs $0.47^\circ$ rotation, $5.4$ vs $8.9$ px focal) and runs about $10^5\times$ faster at about $0.12$ ms per rig. On real data (TotalCapture, CMU Panoptic) it matches or beats offline rig-coupled bundle adjustment on absolute and relative rotation while running four-to-five orders of magnitude faster, and on the Panoptic surround rig it also matches the strongest image-only foundation models (VGGT, VGGT-$\Omega$, $\pi^3$) on relative pose while staying metric and about $15\times$ more accurate in focal length. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: RECALL is a feed-forward method that recalibrates a movable multi-camera rig in a single pass from the OEM calibration and a brief observation of a known object. It is more accurate than bundle adjustment and about 10 to the 5th times faster on synthetic data.
AI.motivation: Rig calibration goes stale when the rig is repositioned or drifts, and classical bundle adjustment needs fresh multi-view captures and a global optimization whose cost grows with the rig, which rules out real-time use.
AI.method: The rig calibration is a shared global rotation composed with per-camera drift. A rig-coupled recurrent operator refines the estimate with differentiable reprojection and cross-camera attention, and a learned Gauss-Newton step solves the shared rotational gauge. Training uses on-the-fly synthetic data without captured datasets.
AI.result: On a synthetic 10-camera benchmark, rotation error is 0.26 degrees versus 0.47 for joint bundle adjustment, focal error is 5.4 versus 8.9 px, and runtime is about 0.12 ms per rig. On TotalCapture and CMU Panoptic it matches or beats offline rig-coupled bundle adjustment and matches VGGT, VGGT-Omega and pi3 on relative pose on the Panoptic rig while staying metric and about 15 times more accurate in focal length.
AI.conclusion: Learned, rig-coupled recalibration can replace slow optimization for real-time online calibration, with training needing only synthetic data.

title: BirdDreams: Joint Perspective and BEV Video Generation for a Plausible, Reactive Driving World Model
summary: Driving world models aim to simulate how a scene unfolds under different ego actions. This requires plausible motion of surrounding vehicles as well as precise ego-trajectory control. Learning vehicle motion from perspective video alone is challenging because motion is entangled with appearance and vehicles can be occluded. Prior work therefore conditions video generation on layouts that specify vehicle motion, providing control over surrounding vehicles but requiring their future trajectories as inputs. We introduce BirdDreams, an autoregressive driving world model that jointly generates perspective video and a schematic bird's-eye-view (BEV) video, making scene layout part of the predicted future. The BEV, rendered from scene annotations for training, depicts roads and vehicles as simple shapes at a fixed metric scale, providing a top-down view of their positions and motion with reduced occlusion between vehicles. Perspective video, by contrast, retains scene details that the BEV omits, such as traffic signals and object appearance. Joint attention between two video diffusion transformers, one per stream, lets each stream inform the other during generation. The predicted BEV also provides a geometric interface for ego control: we translate and rotate its latest frame along an input ego trajectory and use the resulting frames as a soft condition that shows how the scene would appear to move if only the ego vehicle moved. At inference, BirdDreams generates both videos from a single camera image without requiring an HD map or vehicle-state inputs. On PhysicalAI-AV and nuScenes, BirdDreams follows input ego trajectories more faithfully than prior driving world models and generates more plausible ego motion without ego-action conditioning. Human evaluation shows that BirdDreams outperforms a perspective-only baseline in generating realistic surrounding-vehicle behavior.

AI.tldr: BirdDreams is an autoregressive driving world model that jointly generates perspective video and a schematic bird's-eye-view (BEV) video, and uses the BEV as a geometric interface for ego-trajectory control.
AI.motivation: Prior driving world models condition video on layouts that require future vehicle trajectories as input, and perspective-only video entangles vehicle motion with appearance and occlusion.
AI.method: Two video diffusion transformers, one per stream, use joint attention. The BEV is rendered from scene annotations at a fixed metric scale. Ego control translates and rotates the latest BEV frame along an input trajectory and uses the result as a soft condition. Inference needs only a single camera image, with no HD map or vehicle state.
AI.result: On PhysicalAI-AV and nuScenes, BirdDreams follows input ego trajectories more faithfully than prior driving world models and generates more plausible ego motion without ego-action conditioning. Human evaluation finds it beats a perspective-only baseline on realistic surrounding-vehicle behavior.
AI.conclusion: Jointly predicting a BEV layout gives both plausible surrounding-vehicle motion and a usable geometric handle for ego control in driving world models.

title: From Classification to Generation: Vision-Language Models for Roman Imperial Coin Description
summary: Cataloguing a Roman Imperial coin involves reading its legends and identifying its imagery in order to match it to an entry in the standard reference catalogue. Previous work has automated individual parts of this process, such as identifying the issuer or recognizing reverse motifs, by formulating each part as a classification task over a predefined set of labels. We instead formulate coin description as image-to-text generation and adapt an open-weight vision-language model (VLM), Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, to four tasks: transcribing the obverse and reverse legends, and describing the obverse and reverse imagery. To obtain training data, we convert approximately 30,000 auction records into structured image-text pairs. We separate the two sides of each coin, extract and normalize legends and descriptions, and standardize obverse descriptions against a bust-type taxonomy. We then train a separate low-rank adapter for each task on a single 20GB GPU, and evaluate each task with metrics that we define to capture the key components of numismatic descriptions. The adapted models outperform both the unadapted base model and GPT-4.1 on all four tasks, reducing the normalized edit distance of legend transcriptions by over 40% relative to GPT-4.1. The improvement is smaller, but still present, on legends absent from the training data.

AI.tldr: The authors recast Roman Imperial coin cataloguing as image-to-text generation by adapting Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct with a separate LoRA adapter for each of four tasks. The adapted models beat the base model and GPT-4.1 on all four tasks.
AI.motivation: Earlier coin work classified individual attributes such as issuer or reverse motif over predefined labels, which does not produce full catalogue-style descriptions.
AI.method: About 30,000 auction records are converted into structured image-text pairs, with the two sides separated, legends and descriptions normalized, and obverse descriptions standardized to a bust-type taxonomy. A low-rank adapter is trained per task on a single 20GB GPU, and task-specific metrics are defined.
AI.result: The adapted models outperform the unadapted base and GPT-4.1 on all four tasks. Normalized edit distance of legend transcriptions falls by over 40 percent relative to GPT-4.1. The gain is smaller but still present on legends absent from training.
AI.conclusion: Generative VLM adaptation can automate numismatic cataloguing description, with the gains extending partly to unseen legends.

title: Neural Compression for Scientific Particle Data: Perspectives on How Learning Can Help
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures. Extended version of paper accepted at 2026 Conference on Physics and AI (PAI26)
summary: As particle-based simulations grow in scale, efficient compression of scientific data becomes critical. Neural point cloud compression (PCC) methods excel on computer vision (CV) benchmarks, but do they transfer to scientific particle data? We highlight that scientific particles differ from CV point clouds in fractal dimension: CV point clouds are locally planar, but particles are not. This key difference limits the effectiveness of the octree data structure that underpins most PCC methods. Neural codecs achieve only marginal bitrate reductions over the traditional G-PCC baseline on scientific data, revealing a significant performance gap. Supported by an evaluation spanning domains of cosmology, molecular dynamics, and plasma physics, we outline where the structure of scientific data limits current neural approaches and where learning can help in the future.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that neural point cloud compression methods transfer poorly to scientific particle data, because particle sets are not locally planar and so the octree structure underlying these methods is less effective. Neural codecs achieve only marginal gains over G-PCC.
AI.motivation: Neural point cloud compression excels on computer vision benchmarks, but it is unknown whether it works for the growing volume of scientific particle simulations.
AI.method: The authors compare fractal dimension of scientific particles with CV point clouds and evaluate neural codecs against the G-PCC baseline on cosmology, molecular dynamics and plasma physics data.
AI.result: Neural codecs achieve only marginal bitrate reductions over G-PCC on scientific data, revealing a significant performance gap.
AI.conclusion: Structural properties of scientific data limit current neural approaches, and the paper outlines where learning could help in future work.

title: Sophon: A Procedural Diagnostic for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
comment: NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations & Datasets Track). 10 page main text, 44 pages total. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Open-weight Vision-Language Models (VLMs) score 85-94% on spatial benchmarks (BLINK Spatial, What's Up CLEVR) yet collapse to chance on simple geometric questions when object, scene, and texture priors are stripped away. We introduce and open-source Sophon, a procedurally generated diagnostic of paired colored point-cloud stimuli across three coordinate systems (1D linear, 2D Cartesian, 2D polar) and four question types (binary, categorical, comparative, quantitative). Across four open architectures (LLaVA-NeXT, LLaVA-OneVision, Qwen2.5-VL, Idefics3), accuracy clusters at 47-52% while frontier models (Opus 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.4) clear 77-83% and humans reach 84-94%. We use linear probes and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to trace the open-weight failures. Probes of the vision encoder (ViT) and language decoder (LLM) recover Sophon spatial information at 83-85% and 80-86% accuracy, respectively, and the language tower's reasoning circuit answers text-only controls (point clouds as sets of coordinates) at +40 pp over visual stimuli. Language tower per-layer attention attribution localizes visual integration to mid-stack layers. At readout, models elevate the correct answer-set tokens but select among them randomly. We localize the mechanism by tuning individual and grouped components across every architecture's stack, including the vision tower (ViT workspace and reader), the projector, and the language tower (LLM workspace and reader). These experiments demonstrate that this mid-stack workspace holds circuitry capable of organizing the spatial signal so that the frozen reader can decode it. LoRA fine-tuning adjusts that circuitry such that 7B-class VLMs answer Sophon spatial reasoning questions at frontier aggregate accuracy. This work suggests that these models do not have a capability gap for spatial reasoning but suffer from a routing bottleneck that targeted fine-tuning repairs.

AI.tldr: Sophon is an open-source procedural diagnostic of spatial reasoning in VLMs using colored point-cloud stimuli. The authors trace open-weight VLM failures to a mid-stack routing bottleneck that targeted LoRA fine-tuning can repair.
AI.motivation: Open VLMs score 85 to 94 percent on spatial benchmarks yet fall to chance on simple geometric questions once object, scene and texture priors are removed.
AI.method: Sophon generates paired point-cloud stimuli across three coordinate systems and four question types. Linear probes, LoRA and component-level tuning across the ViT and LLM of four open architectures localize the mechanism, and per-layer attention attribution is used on the language tower.
AI.result: Open architectures cluster at 47 to 52 percent accuracy, frontier models reach 77 to 83 percent, and humans reach 84 to 94 percent. Probes recover spatial information at 83 to 85 percent (ViT) and 80 to 86 percent (LLM). Text-only controls beat visual stimuli by 40 points. LoRA fine-tuning brings 7B-class VLMs to frontier aggregate accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The models lack the spatial information but suffer from a routing bottleneck in the mid-stack workspace, which targeted fine-tuning can repair, so the gap is not a capability gap.

title: Paired Geometric Supervision for Generalizable Deepfake Detection
comment: Accepted at BMVC 2026 (poster). 37 pages including supplementary material; 8 figures, 22 tables
summary: We present OrthoPairGTL, a geometric training framework for cross-domain deepfake detection, built on a partially frozen DINOv3 backbone ($\sim$300M parameters), and make three contributions: (1) We re-evaluate six recent transfer-learning detectors (Forensics Adapter, Effort, three GenD variants and FakeSTormer) using the authors' released checkpoints under a single preprocessing pipeline across 17 cross-domain datasets (2018-2025), so that the reported gaps reflect method rather than per-method pipeline tuning. (2) We model the transformation between paired real and fake samples, training Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) adapters with an orthogonal pair decomposition, hyperspherical regularisation, and (in the GSD-LoRA variant) a set-level coherence objective. (3) Under LoRA, this regularisation gives a more stable optimisation profile: GSD-LoRA's post-peak validation degradation is $4.2\times$ shallower than plain LoRA at the same parameter footprint, and the time-averaged validation AUC across training is 1.82 pp higher. On the 17 datasets, GSD-LoRA matches or exceeds every re-evaluated baseline (92.82% vs. 91.58% for the strongest; paired Wilcoxon signed-rank $p=0.015$, 13/17 per-dataset wins), with the largest gains on modern reenactment-heavy benchmarks (DSv1.1, DSv2). Under strict parameter budgets, LayerNorm-only tuning ($\approx$0.03% of the backbone) is the most stable configuration and matches the strongest baseline with a mean of 91.97%.

AI.tldr: OrthoPairGTL is a geometric training framework for cross-domain deepfake detection on a partly frozen DINOv3 backbone, using orthogonal pair decomposition of paired real and fake samples. GSD-LoRA reaches 92.82 percent average accuracy over 17 datasets, above the strongest re-evaluated baseline at 91.58 percent.
AI.motivation: Reported gaps between deepfake detectors may reflect per-method pipeline tuning rather than method differences, and PEFT training on deepfake detection is unstable after peak validation.
AI.method: Six recent transfer-learning detectors are re-evaluated with their released checkpoints under one preprocessing pipeline on 17 cross-domain datasets. PEFT adapters are trained with an orthogonal pair decomposition, hyperspherical regularisation and, in GSD-LoRA, a set-level coherence objective.
AI.result: GSD-LoRA matches or exceeds every baseline (92.82 percent versus 91.58 percent; paired Wilcoxon p = 0.015; 13 of 17 dataset wins), with its post-peak validation degradation 4.2 times shallower than plain LoRA and time-averaged AUC 1.82 points higher. LayerNorm-only tuning (about 0.03 percent of parameters) reaches 91.97 percent mean.
AI.conclusion: Geometric pair supervision gives more stable and generalizable deepfake detection, and very small parameter budgets remain competitive.

title: Honest Fusion Evaluation for Cross-Domain Deepfake Detection: Leakage Audits and Tail Robustness
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027. 19 pages including supplementary material; 6 figures, 10 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Cross-domain video deepfake detection increasingly uses frozen foundation-model experts, combined by calibrated score averaging, a per-video router picking one expert, or a learned head over concatenated features. Expressive routing and feature fusion are often reported to beat plain averaging. Across a 22-dataset frozen-expert testbed, we find those gains are largely evaluation artifacts. A corner theorem locates the gap routing aims to close: because AUC depends only on score ordering, the best any score-space router can do is an oracle reading the test label to pick each video's expert, a ceiling no realisable, label-blind router reaches. The theorem does not order real routers against a calibrated global average; the case against routing is empirical, and no router we test beats that average. Feature fusion reads raw features, falls outside the theorem, and is audited empirically. Reported gains trace to leakage: holding out one dataset leaks siblings sharing identities and reals (over-crediting routing), while holding out one manipulation keeps that dataset's reals in training (over-crediting feature fusion). A $2\times 2$ over fold and evaluation granularity pins the $+2.6$pp feature-fusion "win" to the fold alone: 12/12 significant under leaky folds vs. 0/12 under honest family-held-out folds, where both gains vanish. Fusion still pays off in the tail of hard videos and families: as experts are added, videos every expert misclassifies drop from 15.2% to 2.3%, and global calibrated fusion (InvB) beats the best single expert on worst-family AUC, selective risk (AURC), and low-false-positive recall, stably across protocols. Practitioners should calibrate and combine globally, hold out whole dataset families, and measure tail performance. For score-space routing under ranking metrics, honest evaluation and expert diversity matter more than combiner complexity.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that many gains reported for routing and feature fusion in cross-domain deepfake detection come from leakage in the evaluation protocol, and that global calibrated score averaging matches or beats the routers tested. Fusion still helps on the hardest videos and families.
AI.motivation: Expressive routing and feature fusion are often reported to beat plain averaging of frozen foundation-model experts, but the evaluations may leak information between folds.
AI.method: On a 22-dataset frozen-expert testbed, the authors prove a corner theorem about the AUC ceiling of score-space routers and run leakage audits comparing dataset-held-out and manipulation-held-out folds in a 2 by 2 design over fold and evaluation granularity.
AI.result: The reported +2.6 pp feature-fusion gain is significant in 12 of 12 leaky folds but in 0 of 12 honest family-held-out folds, where both gains vanish. No tested router beats the calibrated global average. As experts are added, videos misclassified by every expert drop from 15.2 percent to 2.3 percent, and global calibrated fusion (InvB) beats the best single expert on worst-family AUC, AURC and low-false-positive recall.
AI.conclusion: Calibrate and combine globally, hold out whole dataset families, and measure tail performance; for score-space routing, honest evaluation and expert diversity matter more than combiner complexity.

title: In-orbit demonstration of object-based change detection applied to the maritime domain
summary: This article presents the successful in-orbit validation of an object-based change detection pipeline for low latency maritime monitoring onboard the CogniSAT-6 mission. We propose and validate a lightweight, three-phase operational sequence: optimized ground-based dual-acquisition scheduling, real-time onboard AI-based vessel segmentation, and multi-temporal matching. Upon acquiring consecutive images over a targeted Area of Interest (AoI), the onboard system correlates vessel detections using a hybrid matching approach that integrates the Hungarian algorithm for optimal assignment with RANSAC-driven spatial and size filters for outlier rejection. A series of in-orbit validations demonstrated robust performance across 11 diverse maritime scenarios, achieving valid recall and precision values (considering only vessel size and location) exceeding 0.8. The validation demonstrated the ability of the system to track both cooperative targets and uncooperative "dark" vessels strictly through geometric consistency. This capacity to autonomously generate and act upon real-time intelligence establishes a foundation for next-generation Insight-as-a-Service (IaaS) and tipping-and-cueing architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper reports in-orbit validation on the CogniSAT-6 mission of an onboard object-based change detection pipeline for maritime monitoring. It achieves recall and precision above 0.8 over 11 maritime scenarios.
AI.motivation: Low-latency maritime monitoring needs onboard processing so that intelligence can be acted on without downlinking all imagery, including detection of dark vessels that do not transmit positions.
AI.method: A three-phase sequence: optimized ground-scheduled dual acquisition, onboard AI vessel segmentation, and multi-temporal matching with the Hungarian algorithm and RANSAC-based spatial and size filters.
AI.result: Across 11 maritime scenarios, recall and precision (considering vessel size and location only) exceed 0.8. The system tracks both cooperative and dark vessels using geometric consistency alone.
AI.conclusion: Onboard change detection establishes a basis for Insight-as-a-Service and tipping-and-cueing architectures.

title: HeadIO: Body-Frame Heading Decomposition for Neural Inertial Odometry on Head-Mounted Devices
summary: Inertial odometry (IO) using only Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) enables camera-free head tracking in head-mounted devices such as VR headsets, AR glasses, and earbuds. Prior IO methods operate in a gravity-aligned world frame, which is not yaw-equivariant. Yaw augmentation improves robustness but does not guarantee equivariance; learned equivariant layers achieve it, but EqNIO's full pipeline costs nearly 3$\times$ the FLOPs of ours. While raw body-frame IMU inputs are inherently yaw-invariant, head tilt redistributes both gravity and motion signals across device axes, making the representation tilt-variant. We propose HeadIO, which combines a body-frame heading decomposition with a bidirectional Mamba backbone for head-mounted inertial odometry. Our decomposition achieves tilt invariance by separating gravity-aligned and horizontal components using only the tilt component of device orientation. We evaluate on four head-mounted datasets and find that HeadIO improves RTE-5s by 8.1% (0.260 m $\to$ 0.239 m) over world-frame methods with learned equivariant layers on Nymeria, the largest benchmark dataset, at nearly 3$\times$ lower FLOPs and 8$\times$ fewer parameters. HeadIO achieves state-of-the-art performance on our primary metric, RTE-5s, on all Aria-glasses datasets, which natively provide body-frame semantics for our decomposition method. We further evaluate the IMU-only deployment scenario on Nymeria, where HeadIO remains state-of-the-art. We show that our method relies mainly on tilt accuracy, which can be obtained from the gravity signal; for yaw, a single-coefficient gyroscope correction removes 11.6% of the yaw error and improves RTE-5s by 2.5%, and sparse external yaw corrections (for example, one every 30 s) can improve RTE-5s by 12.0%. Our decomposition is lightweight, composes with any backbone, and is suitable for real-time deployment on head-mounted devices.

AI.tldr: HeadIO is an IMU-only neural inertial odometry method for head-mounted devices that decomposes body-frame heading and pairs it with a bidirectional Mamba backbone. It improves RTE-5s by 8.1 percent over world-frame methods with learned equivariant layers on Nymeria, at about 3 times lower FLOPs.
AI.motivation: World-frame inertial odometry is not yaw-equivariant, and equivariant pipelines such as EqNIO cost nearly 3 times more FLOPs, while head tilt makes body-frame inputs tilt-variant.
AI.method: A body-frame heading decomposition separates gravity-aligned and horizontal components using only the tilt of device orientation, composed with a bidirectional Mamba backbone.
AI.result: On Nymeria, RTE-5s improves from 0.260 m to 0.239 m, with about 3 times lower FLOPs and 8 times fewer parameters. It achieves state of the art on all Aria-glasses datasets and on IMU-only deployment. A single-coefficient gyroscope yaw correction removes 11.6 percent of yaw error, and sparse external yaw corrections improve RTE-5s by 12.0 percent.
AI.conclusion: Tilt accuracy drives performance, and the lightweight decomposition composes with any backbone for real-time head-mounted deployment.

title: From Pixels to Prompts: Physics-Guided Language Enhancement for AI-Generated Image Detection
summary: AI-generated content (AIGC) has substantially narrowed the visual gap between natural and synthetic images, while existing detectors often rely on generator-specific artifacts and exhibit limited generalization to unseen models. This motivates a fundamental question: which intrinsic physical image characteristics provide stable, discriminative cues for distinguishing natural from AI-generated images? We investigate this by systematically identifying robust physical features and incorporating them into a vision-language representation without external textual prompts at inference. We first analyze 15 handcrafted physical descriptors across images from over 20 generative models. Based on cross-generator stability and real-fake discriminability, we propose a Feature Stability-Discriminability Validation Assessment (FSDVA) to select a compact set of reliable features. Five core features, including Laplacian variance, Sobel statistics, and residual-noise variance, are then used to construct structured textual descriptions encoding physical evidence for CLIP-based learning. We integrate these physics-enriched descriptions with image representations via a native physics-guided multimodal framework, adapting CLIP ViT-L 14 with LoRA. At inference, the model requires only the input image, with no external captions or manual prompts. On GenImage, our method achieves 99.0 percent accuracy on SDv1.4 and 96.7 percent on Wukong, with a mean of 97.23 percent across eight generative models versus 95.8 percent for C2pCLIP under the same setting. On UniversalFakeDetect, it maintains strong, stable generalization across diverse and unseen generation settings. These results show that carefully selected physical image statistics provide complementary forensic evidence to pretrained vision-language representations, enabling interpretable, more generator-agnostic AIGC detection.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a CLIP-based AI-generated image detector that encodes five physical image features, such as Laplacian variance and residual-noise variance, as text descriptions. It reaches 97.23 percent mean accuracy over eight generators on GenImage.
AI.motivation: Existing detectors rely on generator-specific artifacts and generalize poorly to unseen models, so the authors ask which intrinsic physical characteristics give stable cues.
AI.method: Fifteen handcrafted physical descriptors are analyzed across more than 20 generators, and a Feature Stability-Discriminability Validation Assessment (FSDVA) selects five core features. These form structured text descriptions for CLIP ViT-L/14 adapted with LoRA, and no external prompts are needed at inference.
AI.result: On GenImage, accuracy is 99.0 percent on SDv1.4 and 96.7 percent on Wukong, with a mean of 97.23 percent across eight generators versus 95.8 percent for C2pCLIP. On UniversalFakeDetect it generalizes stably to unseen settings.
AI.conclusion: Selected physical statistics provide complementary forensic evidence to pretrained vision-language models, supporting interpretable and more generator-agnostic detection.

title: Lines Are Ideas: Visual Creativity Assessment in Hyperbolic Space
summary: Assessing human creativity from drawings provides a scalable way to evaluate human creative ability. However, existing approaches either rely on costly expert annotation or treat creativity as a single regression target, overlooking its underlying structure. Psychological theories have long emphasized that creativity emerges from balancing novelty and appropriateness. Motivated by this principle, we recast creativity as structured semantic deviation between paired drawings, where novelty measures the extent of departure from the original base sketch, and appropriateness determines whether such departures remain meaningful. This formulation naturally leads to a hyperbolic representation, in which novelty is quantified by geodesic distance and appropriateness is evaluated conditionally via a learned decision boundary, further regulated by an abstraction-conditioned adaptive constraint. Experiments on AuDrA-Drawings demonstrate state-of-the-art alignment with expert judgments and strong robustness under rater and task shifts. Beyond performance gains, our framework reveals an interpretable radial organization of creative variation, offering a principled geometric foundation for automatic creativity assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper recasts visual creativity as structured semantic deviation between paired drawings and assesses it in hyperbolic space, scoring novelty by geodesic distance and appropriateness by a learned decision boundary. It reports state-of-the-art alignment with expert judgments on AuDrA-Drawings.
AI.motivation: Creativity assessment either needs costly expert annotation or treats creativity as a single regression target, ignoring its balance of novelty and appropriateness.
AI.method: Novelty is measured as geodesic distance from the base sketch in hyperbolic representation, appropriateness is evaluated conditionally via a learned decision boundary, and an abstraction-conditioned adaptive constraint regulates the two.
AI.result: On AuDrA-Drawings the method achieves state-of-the-art alignment with expert judgments and robustness under rater and task shifts. It also reveals an interpretable radial organization of creative variation.
AI.conclusion: The geometric formulation offers an interpretable foundation for automatic creativity assessment.

title: Hint-Informed Self-Distillation for Reasoning Segmentation
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. The first two authors contributed equally
summary: Reasoning segmentation requires identifying the target referred to by a query among visually similar objects, yet trajectory-level rewards cannot directly indicate which tokens provide relevant visual evidence. We propose Hint-Informed Self-Distillation (HISD), which uses target-disambiguation evidence for token-level credit assignment. An external model generates Segment Hints offline from training images, queries, and ground-truth target annotations, organizing target identity, discriminative attributes, confusable objects, and anchoring paths. A hint-conditioned exponential moving average teacher scores the student's own trajectories, and HISD computes the teacher-to-student evidence ratio over a token support set to adjust only the magnitudes of positive group-relative advantages, leaving nonpositive advantages unchanged. This design encourages concise reasoning while retaining the information needed for target disambiguation, and the student requires neither hints nor a teacher at inference. Under a unified training protocol, HISD improves ReasonSeg test gIoU and cIoU over our reproduction of DPAD by 3.00 and 3.55 percentage points, respectively. Across the five evaluated splits of ReasonSeg and the RefCOCO family, HISD achieves higher segmentation metrics than this baseline and reduces the average token count of valid reasoning spans by 80.17 to 91.83 percent.

AI.tldr: HISD uses hints generated offline from ground-truth target annotations to give token-level credit in reasoning segmentation. It improves ReasonSeg gIoU and cIoU over a reproduced DPAD baseline by 3.00 and 3.55 points and cuts reasoning token counts by 80 to 92 percent.
AI.motivation: Trajectory-level rewards cannot indicate which tokens carry visual evidence for disambiguating a target among similar objects.
AI.method: An external model produces Segment Hints offline. A hint-conditioned EMA teacher scores the student's trajectories, and the teacher-to-student evidence ratio over a token support set rescales only positive group-relative advantages. The student needs no hints or teacher at inference.
AI.result: Under a unified protocol, HISD improves ReasonSeg test gIoU by 3.00 and cIoU by 3.55 points over the reproduced DPAD. Across five ReasonSeg splits and the RefCOCO family it gives higher segmentation metrics and reduces the average token count of valid reasoning spans by 80.17 to 91.83 percent.
AI.conclusion: Hint-informed self-distillation encourages concise reasoning while keeping the information needed for target disambiguation.

title: Reality Perception Gap: Are AI-Manipulated Video Detectors Ready for the Real World?
summary: AI-manipulated video detectors are typically evaluated on clean, curated datasets. In deployment, however, videos have usually passed through repost compression on social-media platforms and sometimes were captured by imperfect hardware. To measure detection under these conditions, we introduce Reality Perception Gap (RPG), a benchmark of 10,000 videos from frontier generators and partially synthetic edits, processed with cross-platform repost compression and paired with real footage that carries camera-side optical artifacts. RPG also includes socially fragile content, such as crime and wartime footage, where fabricated videos can cause severe social harm. Across 18 detectors, none catches more than 15% of fakes at a 1% false-positive rate. A positive control and a re-encoding sweep separate two sources of failure: generator and content shift degrades detectors before any compression, and repost compression erases the low-level traces that the artifact-based detectors relies on. Existing detectors therefore struggle when deployment conditions strip away the generation artifacts they rely on. These complementary failures suggest that robust detection requires training under deployment conditions and combining low-level, temporal, and semantic evidence, where passive detection may have reached its limits.

AI.tldr: The Reality Perception Gap (RPG) benchmark of 10,000 videos shows that none of 18 AI-manipulated video detectors catches more than 15 percent of fakes at a 1 percent false-positive rate once videos are reposted and compressed.
AI.motivation: Detectors are evaluated on clean, curated data, whereas deployed videos pass through social-media repost compression and often come from imperfect cameras.
AI.method: RPG pairs videos from frontier generators and partial synthetic edits, processed with cross-platform repost compression, with real footage carrying camera optical artifacts. It includes socially fragile content such as crime and wartime footage. A positive control and a re-encoding sweep separate the sources of failure.
AI.result: Across 18 detectors, none catches more than 15 percent of fakes at a 1 percent false-positive rate. Generator and content shift degrade detection even before compression, and repost compression removes the low-level traces that artifact-based detectors use.
AI.conclusion: Robust detection needs training under deployment conditions and combining low-level, temporal and semantic evidence, since passive detection may have reached its limits.

title: RSLiveBench-UAV: A Continually Evolving Vision-Language Benchmark for Aerial Spatial Intelligence
summary: Aerial spatial intelligence (ASI) requires models to understand objects and spatial relationships across changing viewpoints and scales. Evaluating these abilities as models evolve calls for fresh physical observations, yet producing new aerial spatial questions requires repeatedly establishing entity identities, geometric references, and cross-view correspondences. We introduce \textbf{RSLiveBench-UAV}, a continually evolving vision-language benchmark driven by recurring acquisition of real UAV imagery. Its update protocol admits images captured after the preceding release and delays answer disclosure. An entity-centered production workflow uses geometry-assisted association to link repeated observations of physical vehicles, reuse human-verified attributes, and combine them with view-specific annotations and spatial references for traceable question generation. All tasks use deterministic scoring without model judges. We evaluate 30 general-purpose, remote-sensing, and embodied models on 35,491 question records from ten scenes, covering 17 tasks across 2D perception, 3D perception, cross-view perception, and reasoning. All 18 tested embodied models outperform the three selected remote-sensing comparators in Overall, although the strongest embodied model scores 43.29 versus 59.88 for GPT-6-Astra. Fine-grained vehicle recognition remains challenging, and performance varies across heights and camera pitches. Retrospective scene-group comparisons and rolling-window replay characterize score-pattern consistency under scene renewal. RSLiveBench-UAV connects fresh physical observations, entity-centered answer production, and systematic model evaluation to support continual assessment of ASI. Benchmark will release at this https URL

AI.tldr: RSLiveBench-UAV is a continually evolving vision-language benchmark built from recurring UAV imagery, with delayed answer disclosure and deterministic scoring. Over 35,491 questions, the strongest embodied model scores 43.29 against 59.88 for GPT-6-Astra.
AI.motivation: Evaluating aerial spatial intelligence as models evolve requires fresh physical observations, and writing new spatial questions repeatedly is costly.
AI.method: An entity-centered production workflow uses geometry-assisted association to link repeated observations of vehicles, reuses human-verified attributes and adds view-specific annotations and spatial references. All tasks use deterministic scoring without model judges.
AI.result: Thirty models are evaluated on 35,491 questions from ten scenes across 17 tasks. All 18 tested embodied models outperform the three remote-sensing comparators on Overall, but the best embodied model scores 43.29 against 59.88 for GPT-6-Astra. Fine-grained vehicle recognition is hard, and performance varies with height and camera pitch.
AI.conclusion: Continual benchmarking with fresh observations supports ongoing assessment of aerial spatial intelligence, with score patterns checked under scene renewal.

title: Validation of a Facial-Video Digital Hydration Biomarker Score for Tracking Hydration State Transitions in a Real-World Fasting Model
summary: Hydration influences physiology and daily function, yet repeated practical measurement in everyday settings remains limited. We present initial real-world evidence that a facial-video lifestyle digital biomarker score can track the direction of hydration state transitions. Using Ramadan fasting as a model of prolonged fluid abstinence, we assessed whether the score tracks the transition between the fasting (pre-drink) state and the rehydrated (post-drink) state across three validation layers. In the primary cohort (104 participants, 208 videos), the score increased from a mean of 36.6 in the fasting (pre-drink) state to 70.6 in the rehydrated (post-drink) state (change = +33.9, 95% CI [+30.7, +37.1], p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 2.03), with 102 of 104 participants (98.1%) showing an upward shift. In a nested body-weight subgroup (20 participants), body weight increased by +0.74 kg after fluid intake (p < 0.001), confirming fluid uptake and providing supportive physical anchoring. In a nested serum osmolality subgroup (10 participants), osmolality decreased by -5.1 mOsm/kg (p < 0.001), with all post-drink values within the normal clinical range, providing exploratory biological support. An exploratory secondary comparison of water versus electrolyte rehydration showed no statistically significant difference in short-term score change (p = 0.247). This study does not establish a clinical diagnostic test for dehydration. Rather, these findings support the score as a lifestyle digital biomarker for tracking the direction of hydration state change in real-world settings.

AI.tldr: A facial-video hydration biomarker score rises from 36.6 in the fasting state to 70.6 after rehydration in 104 participants, and tracks the direction of hydration change. The authors present it as a lifestyle biomarker, not a clinical diagnostic test.
AI.motivation: Repeated practical hydration measurement in everyday settings is limited, and Ramadan fasting offers a model of prolonged fluid abstinence.
AI.method: A facial-video digital biomarker score is compared before and after drinking across three validation layers: the primary cohort (104 participants, 208 videos), a body-weight subgroup (20 participants) and a serum osmolality subgroup (10 participants). An exploratory comparison looks at water versus electrolyte rehydration.
AI.result: The score rises by +33.9 (95 percent CI +30.7 to +37.1, p below 0.001, Cohen's d 2.03), and 102 of 104 participants shift upward. Body weight rises by 0.74 kg and osmolality falls by 5.1 mOsm/kg, both p below 0.001. Water and electrolyte rehydration do not differ significantly (p = 0.247).
AI.conclusion: The score tracks the direction of hydration state change in real-world settings, supporting its use as a lifestyle digital biomarker, not a diagnostic test.

title: Federated Class Incremental Learning: A Pseudo Feature Based Approach Without Exemplars
summary: Federated learning often assumes that data is fixed in advance, which is unrealistic in many real-world scenarios where new data continuously arrives, causing catastrophic forgetting. To address this challenge, we propose FCLPF (Federated Class Incremental Learning with Pseudo Features), a method that uses pseudo features generated from prototypes to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. Our approach reduces communication costs and improves efficiency by eliminating the need for past data and avoiding computationally heavy models like GANs. Experimental results on CIFAR-100 show that FCLPF achieves an average accuracy of 51.87% and an average forgetting of 9.62%, significantly outperforming existing baselines with an average accuracy of 47.72% and forgetting of 20.46%. On TinyImageNet, FCLPF achieves 37.56% accuracy and 3.14% forgetting, compared to the baselines' 27.69% accuracy and 24.46% forgetting, demonstrating the superior performance of FCLPF.

AI.tldr: FCLPF is a federated class-incremental learning method that generates pseudo features from class prototypes to reduce forgetting without storing exemplars or using GANs. It reports higher accuracy and lower forgetting than baselines on CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet.
AI.motivation: In federated learning with arriving data, catastrophic forgetting is a problem, and existing approaches need past data or heavy generative models with high communication costs.
AI.method: Pseudo features are generated from class prototypes, which removes the need for past data and avoids computationally heavy generators such as GANs.
AI.result: On CIFAR-100, FCLPF reaches 51.87 percent average accuracy and 9.62 percent average forgetting, versus 47.72 percent and 20.46 percent for baselines. On TinyImageNet it reaches 37.56 percent accuracy and 3.14 percent forgetting, versus 27.69 percent and 24.46 percent.
AI.conclusion: Prototype-based pseudo features offer an exemplar-free and communication-efficient route to reducing forgetting in federated class-incremental learning.

title: Back to the Question: Tracing Visual Distraction Through Text Tokens
summary: The visual world is cluttered: robust vision-language reasoning requires ignoring irrelevant information. Yet vision-language models (VLMs) can suffer substantial accuracy losses when answering questions about a target image with distractors present. Existing mitigations focus on selecting relevant images or limiting information exchange between images. Through a systematic analysis of three open 7-8B VLMs on five perception benchmarks adapted to include distractor images, we show that distractors reduce accuracy even when models correctly identify the relevant image, suggesting that selection alone is not enough. To understand the mechanism behind this interference, we combine attention analysis with targeted knockouts in Qwen2.5-VL and identify middle-layer distractor-to-text connections as a pathway through which irrelevant visual information affects reasoning. We introduce answer consistency regularization, which encourages consistent answer distributions with and without distractors. Without directly constraining attention, this objective reduces middle-layer attention from question tokens to distractor images, consistent with the pathway our analysis implicates. With five distractors, our approach improves circular accuracy by an average of 16 percentage points over the Qwen2.5-VL baseline across the five benchmarks while preserving single-image performance.

AI.tldr: The paper traces visual distraction in VLMs to middle-layer distractor-to-text attention connections in Qwen2.5-VL, and introduces answer consistency regularization, which improves circular accuracy by 16 points on average with five distractors.
AI.motivation: VLMs lose accuracy when distractor images are present, even when they select the relevant image, so image selection alone is not enough.
AI.method: Attention analysis and targeted knockouts in Qwen2.5-VL locate the pathway. Answer consistency regularization encourages consistent answer distributions with and without distractors, and reduces middle-layer attention from question tokens to distractor images without constraining attention directly.
AI.result: With five distractors, circular accuracy improves by an average of 16 percentage points over the Qwen2.5-VL baseline across five perception benchmarks, while single-image performance is preserved.
AI.conclusion: Distractor interference flows through identifiable middle-layer connections, and consistency-based training can reduce it without explicit attention constraints.

title: Estimating Image Creativity
summary: What makes an image creative? Although this may seem like a highly subjective decision, research in psychology suggests that creativity may be based on a set of fundamental creativity dimensions such as novelty, surprise, and arousal. A deeper understanding of image creativity can benefit both research and practical applications. Exploring how human viewers use creativity dimensions to evaluate image creativity may allow us to predict a target image's human-rated creativity automatically. We present a novel framework to estimate the perceived creativity of an image by: (1) predicting the strengths of an image's novelty, surprise, and arousal creativity dimensions, and (2) combining the creativity dimension strengths to estimate an image creativity score. Controlled human-subject experiments were conducted on Amazon Mechanical Turk to collect data to train supervised machine learning models to estimate an image's strengths on the three creativity dimensions. A final machine learning model takes the predicted dimension strengths as input to produce an estimated image creativity score. Results showed that our estimated creativity scores are statistically equivalent to human ratings of creativity for the images we tested. The novel contributions of our research are: (1) identification and validation of three psychological creativity dimensions used to estimate image creativity; (2) supervised machine learning models to automatically estimate novelty, surprise, and arousal strengths for an input image; (3) a supervised machine learning model to predict a creativity score from novelty, surprise, and arousal strengths for an input image, and (4) experimental methods to confirm the accuracy, advantages, and limitations of our approach.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework that estimates image creativity by predicting novelty, surprise and arousal strengths and combining them into a score. Estimated scores are statistically equivalent to human ratings on the tested images.
AI.motivation: Image creativity may be decomposed into psychologically grounded dimensions, and predicting them could automate creativity assessment for research and applications.
AI.method: Controlled Mechanical Turk experiments collect human ratings used to train supervised models for novelty, surprise and arousal, and a final model maps these to an overall creativity score.
AI.result: The estimated creativity scores are statistically equivalent to human ratings for the tested images. The paper validates three creativity dimensions and gives supervised models for each dimension and for the overall score.
AI.conclusion: Psychological creativity dimensions can be predicted from images and combined into a creativity estimate, with stated advantages and limitations.

title: Saying No by Asking Yes: Affirmative Decomposition and Evidence Reflection for Frozen CLIP
summary: Frozen vision-language models often match concepts mentioned in a caption without respecting their negation: a query "a kitchen with no toaster" favors an image containing a toaster. Yet these models are substantially stronger at matching affirmative descriptions. We exploit this asymmetry with Negation-Aware Evidence Scoring (NAES), which reformulates negated descriptions into affirmative queries and combines their evidence by caption structure. A lightweight text decomposer, NegSplit, identifies this structure by extracting negated spans and the remaining affirmative context. For captions with an affirmative remainder, NAES matches that content and applies a presence-based correction for the denial. When no affirmative content remains, it queries the denied object's presence and reflects the evidence around a reference to score the negated description. With LAION-2B CLIP, NAES achieves 82.4% accuracy on COCO-MCQ and 93.0% on VOC2007-MCQ, surpassing KTN by 2.9 and 0.9 percentage points; with OpenAI CLIP, it exceeds PeakPatch accuracy by 4.4 and 26.0 points, respectively. NAES also improves negated-description retrieval on COCO and MSR-VTT, with gains extending to SigLIP, SigLIP 2, and larger CLIP encoders. The strongest multiple-choice results use competing descriptions to center and align evidence; retrieval improvements persist without this conditioning. These findings show that explicitly separating affirmative matching from denied-object evidence can substantially improve negation-aware ranking.

AI.tldr: NAES handles negation in frozen CLIP by rewriting negated descriptions as affirmative queries and presence checks, with NegSplit as the decomposer. It reaches 82.4 percent on COCO-MCQ and 93.0 percent on VOC2007-MCQ with LAION-2B CLIP.
AI.motivation: Frozen CLIP models match negated captions such as "a kitchen with no toaster" to images containing the denied object, although they are stronger on affirmative descriptions.
AI.method: NegSplit extracts negated spans and the remaining affirmative context. If affirmative content remains, NAES matches it and applies a presence-based correction for the denial. Otherwise it queries the denied object's presence and reflects the evidence around a reference.
AI.result: With LAION-2B CLIP, NAES reaches 82.4 percent on COCO-MCQ and 93.0 percent on VOC2007-MCQ, surpassing KTN by 2.9 and 0.9 points. With OpenAI CLIP it exceeds PeakPatch by 4.4 and 26.0 points. It also improves negated retrieval on COCO and MSR-VTT, with gains extending to SigLIP and SigLIP 2.
AI.conclusion: Separating affirmative matching from denied-object evidence substantially improves negation-aware ranking for frozen vision-language models.

title: Test-Time Selective Adaptation for Cross-Modal UAV Object Tracking with Token Shift
summary: Cross-modal unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) object tracking faces modality-induced appearance discrepancies and abrupt target-position shifts that can arise from modality switching, UAV motion, and inter-sensor offsets. Although existing methods model modality and spatial variations, they primarily rely on offline representation learning and offer limited localization-oriented adaptation during testing. To address these challenges, we propose Test-Time Selective Adaptation with Token Shift (TSAT), which derives spatial and temporal adaptation signals from unlabeled test sequences for online optimization. Specifically, we design a controllable token shift auxiliary task, which imposes explicit spatial correspondence between predefined token translations and resultant localization offsets, generating stable annotation-free spatial adaptation signals. Furthermore, we introduce a temporal backward prediction auxiliary task to exploit frame-wise temporal dependencies, effectively mitigating cumulative localization errors in continuous tracking. To suppress interference from unreliable tracking samples, we develop a reliability-aware update gating strategy to screen valid adaptation signals and stabilize online parameter updates. Experiments on CM-UOT demonstrate that TSAT achieves state-of-the-art performance against existing test-time adaptation methods, exhibiting superior robustness under frequent modality switching and severe spatial displacement. Experiments across tracking frameworks and datasets further validate the effectiveness and generalization capability of TSAT.

AI.tldr: TSAT performs test-time adaptation for cross-modal UAV tracking using a controllable token-shift auxiliary task and a temporal backward prediction task, with reliability-aware gating of updates. It achieves state-of-the-art results on CM-UOT.
AI.motivation: Cross-modal UAV tracking suffers from appearance discrepancies between modalities and abrupt position shifts, and existing methods adapt poorly at test time.
AI.method: Unlabeled test sequences supply spatial adaptation signals through token translations matched to localization offsets, and temporal signals through backward prediction. A reliability-aware update gate screens adaptation signals before online parameter updates.
AI.result: TSAT achieves state-of-the-art performance against existing test-time adaptation methods on CM-UOT, with superior robustness under frequent modality switching and severe spatial displacement. Results generalize across tracking frameworks and datasets.
AI.conclusion: Annotation-free online adaptation with reliability gating improves cross-modal UAV tracking robustness.

title: DiFiT: Distribution-Fidelity-guided Visual Token Pruning for Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of multimodal large language models, but answer accuracy only partly reflects its effect. Pruning can change the probabilities of alternative response tokens even when greedy answers remain correct and unchanged. We compare full and pruned response distributions under shared reference prefixes. Average predictive drift grows with compression on fixed correctly answered samples. Separate analyses associate larger drift with more confidence-decision disagreements and sampling failures. We propose DiFiT (Distribution-Fidelity-guided Token pruning) to learn discrete selection from reference answers and full-token response distributions. Dual-View Distillation matches probabilities across the vocabulary, while answer supervision supports task quality. A learned scorer and differentiable Top-$K$ learn which visual evidence to retain. A multi-budget mask objective supports different retention ratios through one shared ranking over a frozen model. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, DiFiT reduces sampling-induced negative flips by 30.3% relative to FastV at 10% retention on four-task greedy-correct controls. It preserves 98.74% of baseline performance on MME at 30% retention.

AI.tldr: DiFiT prunes visual tokens in multimodal LLMs by learning selection from full-token response distributions rather than answers alone. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B it cuts sampling-induced negative flips by 30.3 percent relative to FastV at 10 percent retention and keeps 98.74 percent of MME performance at 30 percent retention.
AI.motivation: Visual token pruning changes alternative response probabilities even when greedy answers stay correct, and answer accuracy alone does not reflect this drift.
AI.method: Full and pruned response distributions are compared under shared reference prefixes. DiFiT uses Dual-View Distillation to match probabilities across the vocabulary, answer supervision, a learned scorer and differentiable Top-K, and a multi-budget mask objective over a frozen model.
AI.result: On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, sampling-induced negative flips fall by 30.3 percent relative to FastV at 10 percent retention on four-task greedy-correct controls. It preserves 98.74 percent of baseline performance on MME at 30 percent retention.
AI.conclusion: Distribution fidelity is a useful objective for visual token pruning, and one learned ranking can serve multiple retention budgets.

title: SAVE: Less is More in Agentic Video Reasoning
summary: Agentic video-reasoning frameworks iteratively explore a video, choosing what to observe based on the query and evidence gathered so far. Existing methods are typically evaluated with different backbones, preprocessing pipelines, and computational budgets, making it difficult to determine which components actually drive performance, how much they cost, and whether agentic inference is preferable to native video reasoning in the first place. We conduct a controlled evaluation of a diverse set of recent agentic video-reasoning systems across two strong contemporary backbones, with explicit token and monetary-cost accounting. Across Gemini 3 Flash and Gemma 4, most existing agentic frameworks fail to consistently improve over native video inference and often increase computational cost. We investigate two primary questions: (1) How much agentic framework complexity is necessary for effective video reasoning? (2) When, if at all, is agentic video reasoning preferable to just using the backbone directly? To answer the first question, we introduce a deliberately minimal Active Exploration Baseline and show that it remains competitive with substantially more elaborate agents. We then propose targeted extensions to this baseline, yielding SAVE (Simple Agentic Video Explorer). SAVE outperforms all evaluated prior agentic methods in five of six backbone-benchmark settings. Turning to the second question, our results indicate that the advantage of agentic exploration grows when dense processing would otherwise represent answer-relevant events too sparsely, particularly for long videos and temporally concentrated evidence. Overall, our results suggest that agentic video reasoning should favor simple frameworks over increasingly elaborate pipelines and focus primarily on long-form video, where selective evidence acquisition offers the clearest advantage over native inference.

AI.tldr: SAVE is a simple agentic video explorer built on a minimal Active Exploration Baseline. It beats prior agentic methods in five of six backbone-benchmark settings, and agentic exploration helps most on long videos with temporally concentrated evidence.
AI.motivation: Agentic video-reasoning systems are compared under different backbones, preprocessing and budgets, so it is unclear which components matter, what they cost, and whether they beat native video inference.
AI.method: A controlled evaluation across Gemini 3 Flash and Gemma 4 with explicit token and monetary-cost accounting. A minimal Active Exploration Baseline is introduced, then extended to SAVE.
AI.result: Most existing agentic frameworks fail to consistently improve over native video inference and often raise cost. SAVE outperforms all evaluated prior agentic methods in five of six backbone-benchmark settings. Agentic exploration helps most on long videos where dense processing represents answer-relevant events too sparsely.
AI.conclusion: Agentic video reasoning should favor simple frameworks and be focused on long-form video, where selective evidence acquisition has the clearest advantage.

title: Prediction or Persistence? What Future-Prediction Scores Miss About World Models
comment: Accepted at the CoRL 2026 Workshop "Do Robots Need World Models?"
summary: Pretrained video world models are compared and chosen as components for robot learning largely by future-prediction scores. On its own, such a score cannot be read as evidence of prediction, because it mixes encoder quality, the near future's resemblance to the recent past, and the predictor's own contribution. We separate the three with a matched control.
