title: Description-Guided CLIP Adaptation with Local Evidence Calibration for Few-Shot Plant Disease Recognition
summary: Accurate plant disease recognition is essential for intelligent agriculture, but few-shot settings provide limited labeled samples that may not capture diagnostic symptoms and intra-class variations. Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, offer transferable visual-semantic knowledge. However, existing CLIP-based methods often rely on coarse class semantics and global visual representations, overlooking disease-specific diagnostic information and fine-grained local cues. Excessive few-shot adaptation may also cause over-specialization and weaken the generalization ability of large-scale pre-training. We propose a description-guided, two-stage CLIP adaptation method to address these issues. Symptom and comparative descriptions enrich class semantics with typical visual symptoms and discriminative cues between similar diseases. The enhanced semantics guide the aggregation of class-relevant patch evidence to calibrate global image-text matching with fine-grained cues. For adaptation, we first update the vision-language encoders with lightweight parameters, then freeze them and train a linear classifier. At inference, the classifier is used for in-domain prediction, while class prototypes from the adapted text encoder support cross-domain prediction and retain vision-language transferability. Experiments with two backbones show that our method achieves the highest mean accuracy in most few-shot settings on PlantVillage, Cassava, and Pear, reaching 93.16%, 79.30%, and 96.56%, respectively, with ViT-L/14 under 16-shot. On class-aligned cross-domain evaluation across 21 shared PlantDoc classes, it achieves 56.96% accuracy, outperforming all compared methods. These results demonstrate its effectiveness in fine-grained few-shot plant disease recognition and cross-domain generalization.

AI.tldr: A description-guided two-stage CLIP adaptation method for few-shot plant disease recognition, which enriches class semantics with symptom descriptions and calibrates image-text matching with class-relevant patch evidence. It reports the highest mean accuracy in most few-shot settings and 56.96% cross-domain accuracy on PlantDoc.
AI.motivation: Few-shot CLIP methods rely on coarse class semantics and global representations, so they overlook disease-specific symptoms and fine-grained local cues, and excessive adaptation weakens generalisation.
AI.method: Symptom and comparative descriptions enrich class semantics with typical symptoms and discriminative cues between similar diseases. These guide aggregation of class-relevant patch evidence to calibrate global image-text matching. The vision-language encoders are first updated with lightweight parameters, then frozen, and a linear classifier is trained. Class prototypes from the adapted text encoder support cross-domain prediction.
AI.result: With ViT-L/14 under 16-shot, accuracy reaches 93.16% on PlantVillage, 79.30% on Cassava and 96.56% on Pear. On cross-domain evaluation across 21 shared PlantDoc classes it reaches 56.96%, outperforming all compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Description-guided local evidence calibration improves fine-grained few-shot plant disease recognition and cross-domain generalisation while keeping the pretrained transferability.

title: RADIANT: Redundancy-Aware Information Allocation for Universal Multi-Modal Fusion
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures. Published in ACM Multimedia 2026 (MM '26). Code: this https URL
summary: Universal multi-modal fusion often fails not because modalities are insufficiently aligned, but because the fusion process allocates information poorly: redundant evidence is repeatedly amplified, modality-unique evidence is over-smoothed during alignment, and task-dependent synergistic evidence is insufficiently activated. We present RADIANT (Redundancy-Aware Dynamic Information Allocation Network), a task-general framework that organizes fusion around three complementary roles: suppressing redundant cross-modal overlap, preserving modality-unique evidence, and composing task-conditioned synergy through cross-modal interaction. Specifically, stable matrix-exponential projections are used to reduce interference among shared and modality-unique streams, while task memory with hard positive updates selects which synergistic interactions should be activated for the current fusion regime. Extensive experiments across six heterogeneous fusion tasks show consistent improvements over the compared methods. On FLIR, RADIANT improves downstream detection mAP@0.5 from 91.2% to 96.8%, a gain of 5.6 percentage points (6.1% relative) over GIF. RADIANT also exhibits strong direct cross-dataset transfer, with further gains from inference-time task-memory adaptation while keeping all network weights frozen. Additional ablations and sensitivity studies support the robustness of the allocation mechanism.

AI.tldr: RADIANT is a task-general multi-modal fusion framework that suppresses redundant cross-modal overlap, preserves modality-unique evidence and activates task-conditioned synergy. It improves FLIR detection mAP@0.5 from 91.2% to 96.8% over six heterogeneous fusion tasks.
AI.motivation: Fusion often fails because it allocates information poorly, not because modalities are misaligned: redundant evidence is amplified, unique evidence is over-smoothed during alignment, and synergistic evidence is under-activated.
AI.method: Matrix-exponential projections reduce interference between shared and modality-unique streams. A task memory with hard positive updates selects which synergistic interactions to activate for the current fusion regime.
AI.result: Across six heterogeneous fusion tasks RADIANT shows consistent improvements. On FLIR, downstream detection mAP@0.5 rises from 91.2% to 96.8%, a gain of 5.6 points (6.1% relative) over GIF. It transfers across datasets, with further gains from inference-time task-memory adaptation while network weights stay frozen.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly allocating information between redundant, unique and synergistic streams improves universal multi-modal fusion, with robustness supported by ablations and sensitivity studies.

title: TransXplainRRG: A Radiologist-Evaluated LVLM for Chest Radiograph Report Generation
summary: Recent advancements in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLM) enhance X-ray report generation, but often neglect clinical context, overlook workflow integration, and lack explainability, which hinders clinical adoption due to interpretability and reliability concerns. This paper addresses the dual challenges of performance and expert explainability in automated X-ray report generation for clinical AI applications. Our proposed approach, TransXplainRRG, utilises an off-the-shelf Swin Transformer model along with a transformer-based text encoder that incorporates patient medical history to generate a radiology report. Further, we explore an expert-guided `inside-out' approach and extract only abnormal findings for radiology report refinement. Thus, this study bridges the gap between high-performance automation and interpretability critical for clinical practice by combining state-of-the-art transformer-based vision encoders, text encoders, and LLMs. TransXplainRRG is trained and tested on the large-scale MIMIC-CXR dataset and further evaluated on the unseen IU X-Ray dataset to demonstrate its generalizability and robustness. We employed the GREEN metric as a complementary measure of clinical consistency, achieving scores of 0.327 on MIMIC-CXR and 0.605 on IU X-Ray, both higher than those achieved by MAIRA-2 under the same evaluation setting. It also performed competitively across standard evaluation metrics, frequently matching or surpassing state-of-the-art models. Additionally, we introduce qualitative evaluation metrics developed from radiologists' viewpoints and conduct a preliminary radiologist evaluation on 100 generated reports to assess their clinical relevance. Quantitative and qualitative analyses further demonstrate the potential of our TransXplainRRG framework for reliable and explainable radiology report generation.

AI.tldr: TransXplainRRG is a chest radiograph report generation model that uses a Swin Transformer, a text encoder over patient history, and expert-guided refinement of abnormal findings. It reports GREEN scores of 0.327 on MIMIC-CXR and 0.605 on IU X-Ray, both higher than MAIRA-2 under the same setting, and a preliminary radiologist evaluation of 100 reports.
AI.motivation: LVLM-based X-ray report generation often ignores clinical context and workflow, and lacks explainability, which hinders clinical adoption.
AI.method: The model uses an off-the-shelf Swin Transformer and a transformer-based text encoder that incorporates patient medical history. An expert-guided inside-out approach extracts only abnormal findings for report refinement. The approach combines vision encoders, text encoders and LLMs.
AI.result: Trained on MIMIC-CXR and tested on the unseen IU X-Ray dataset, the model scores 0.327 on MIMIC-CXR and 0.605 on IU X-Ray with GREEN, both higher than MAIRA-2 under the same evaluation. It performs competitively on standard metrics, frequently matching or surpassing state-of-the-art models. A radiologist evaluation covers 100 generated reports.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a path to reliable and explainable report generation, although the radiologist evaluation is preliminary.

title: FuGIBench: Evaluating Reliable Preparation in Streaming Video
summary: An assistant watching a worker can prepare for an emerging need before the worker is ready to receive this http URL the need evolves, the assistant must maintain preparation until a response is due, or withdraw it if the need disappears. Video anticipation and interactive response benchmarks leave this interval between early evidence and response largely unmeasured. We introduce FuGIBench (Future-Grounded Interaction), a streaming-video benchmark in which a model chooses among waiting, reversible preparation, and response given a causal video prefix and a task contract. The benchmark contains 19,893 synthetic tool-assistance videos across ten tool tasks, in handover, ordinary-activity, and cancelled-need tracks. One primary score credits sustained preparation, incorporates response-interval alignment, and penalizes activity when the reference prescribes waiting. On a frozen set of 1,000 episodes, a reference system with a longer preparation lead has poorer response alignment, while similar handover leads accompany different levels of activity during ordinary work in matched scenarios. Together with cancellation analyses, these results show why evaluating preparation requires tracking decisions as needs develop, become actionable, or disappear.

AI.tldr: FuGIBench is a streaming-video benchmark in which a model chooses among waiting, reversible preparation and response, scored by one primary metric that credits sustained preparation and response-interval alignment. It shows that evaluating preparation requires tracking decisions as needs develop, become actionable or disappear.
AI.motivation: An assistant watching a worker should prepare before the worker needs help, maintain that preparation until a response is due, and withdraw it if the need disappears. Existing video anticipation and interactive response benchmarks do not measure this interval.
AI.method: The benchmark has 19,893 synthetic tool-assistance videos across ten tool tasks, in handover, ordinary-activity and cancelled-need tracks. Given a causal video prefix and a task contract, a model chooses among waiting, reversible preparation and response. The primary score penalises activity when the reference prescribes waiting. Analyses include cancellation.
AI.result: On a frozen set of 1,000 episodes, a reference system with a longer preparation lead has poorer response alignment. Similar handover leads accompany different levels of activity during ordinary work in matched scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Preparation should be evaluated over time, and tracking decisions across the need's lifecycle, including cancellation, reveals behaviour that single-point metrics miss.

title: Teach with Blinks: Breaking Linguistic Momentum in On-Policy Distillation for Fine-Grained Multimodal Perception
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as an effective post-training approach to improving fine-grained perception in multimodal large language models by amortizing costly inference-time zooming operations into a single-pass recipe. However, vanilla OPD is inherently susceptible to linguistic momentum: the teacher can follow the student's erroneous prefixes, thus weakening corrective supervision. To address this, we propose Blink On-Policy Distillation (BlinkOPD), in which the teacher "blinks" at every token: it reads the same prefix once with its eyes open and once with its eyes closed. A first-glance gain further strengthens the correction on rollouts that conflict with the teacher. By extracting more effective supervision from each on-policy trajectory, BlinkOPD achieves state-of-the-art average performance across six fine-grained benchmarks using only 500 training images (12x less data) than existing OPD methods. Beyond fine-grained perception, BlinkOPD also demonstrates strong zero-shot improvements across ten held-out benchmarks spanning general visual perception, visual hallucination, and multimodal reasoning abilities. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: BlinkOPD is an on-policy distillation method for fine-grained multimodal perception that counters linguistic momentum by having the teacher read each prefix both with eyes open and with eyes closed. It reaches state-of-the-art average performance on six fine-grained benchmarks with 12x less data (500 images).
AI.motivation: Vanilla on-policy distillation is susceptible to linguistic momentum: the teacher follows the student's erroneous prefixes, which weakens corrective supervision.
AI.method: At every token the teacher reads the same prefix once with its eyes open and once with its eyes closed. A first-glance gain strengthens the correction on rollouts that conflict with the teacher. This extracts more supervision from each on-policy trajectory.
AI.result: BlinkOPD achieves state-of-the-art average performance across six fine-grained benchmarks using only 500 training images, 12 times less data than existing OPD methods. It also shows zero-shot improvements on ten held-out benchmarks covering general perception, visual hallucination and multimodal reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Contrasting open-eye and closed-eye teacher readings yields stronger supervision per trajectory, improving fine-grained perception with far less data and transferring to other capabilities.

title: Gravity and Flight: Learning to Navigate Fine-Grained Remote Sensing Scenes
summary: Vision-language models are increasingly capable, yet their reasoning in complex remote sensing scenes can remain coarse-grained and insufficiently grounded in task-relevant visual evidence. We propose Gravity and Flight (G&F), a framework for scene specialization with limited supervision that separates visual and reasoning verification while coupling policy updates. It combines Evidence-of-Thought supervised fine-tuning (EoT-SFT) and Relational Transfer Policy Optimization (RTPO). EoT-SFT teaches fine-grained observation and faithful reasoning through description, analysis, and supported conclusions. RTPO independently samples responses to scene-matched image pairs with fine-grained visual differences under a shared task. Its rubric-based verification combines Gravity, which checks visual fidelity and description coverage, and Flight, which takes descriptions as premises to assess evidence use and relations between paired judgments. Their scores and task correctness yield a shared pair-level advantage that couples policy updates from both responses. Using 1,008 demonstrations and 500 training pairs for harbor specialization, G&F achieves a mean score of 69.12 across six evaluation sets, exceeding the backbone and supervised initialization by 9.76 and 4.56 points. Matched controls show gains over single-image and joint-input RL, and removing either verification view reduces performance. Applying G&F to urban specialization also improves on the base model and supervised initialization across three evaluation subsets. Project details and updates are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Gravity and Flight is a framework for specialising vision-language models to remote sensing scenes, combining EoT-SFT for evidence-based reasoning with RTPO, a pair-level policy optimisation that couples two verification views. It reaches a mean score of 69.12 across six evaluation sets, exceeding the backbone by 9.76 points.
AI.motivation: VLM reasoning in complex remote sensing scenes is coarse-grained and insufficiently grounded in task-relevant visual evidence, and scene specialisation must work with limited supervision.
AI.method: EoT-SFT teaches fine-grained observation and faithful reasoning through description, analysis and supported conclusions. RTPO samples responses to scene-matched image pairs with fine-grained differences. Gravity checks visual fidelity and description coverage, and Flight takes descriptions as premises to assess evidence use and relations between paired judgements. Their scores and task correctness give a shared pair-level advantage that couples the policy updates.
AI.result: Using 1,008 demonstrations and 500 training pairs for harbour specialisation, G&F reaches a mean score of 69.12 across six evaluation sets, exceeding the backbone and supervised initialisation by 9.76 and 4.56 points. Matched controls outperform single-image and joint-input RL, and removing either verification view reduces performance. Urban specialisation also improves on the base model.
AI.conclusion: Coupling two verification views in pair-level policy optimisation improves grounded reasoning for remote sensing specialisation with limited supervision.

title: RICapBench: A Fine-Grained Visual Understanding Benchmark Dataset for Vision-Language Models in Remote Sensing
summary: Advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have improved remote sensing image analysis and supported geospatial decision-making. However, fine-grained understanding of remote sensing imagery remains challenging for VLMs. Large variations in object scale, complex geospatial relations among instances, and limited visual detail hinder precise instance localization, visible attribute identification, and spatial relation understanding, potentially leading to descriptions that lack visual grounding. Existing datasets and benchmarks insufficiently assess end-to-end instance localization and captioning without target-specific textual cues. To support this evaluation, we introduce RICapBench, a dataset and benchmark that unifies instance localization and fine-grained captioning in remote sensing. RICapBench contains 245,466 instance-level annotations and 498,005 spatial relation tuples spanning general remote sensing, UAV remote sensing, and dense small-object scenarios. Each annotation pairs an object's oriented bounding box with a natural language description of its visible attributes and spatial relations to surrounding instances and environmental elements. To evaluate the accuracy and completeness of spatial relation captioning, we propose a remote sensing spatial relation parser and the RelCap-F1 metric. We combine RelCap-F1 with instance localization and attribute captioning metrics into a composite metric, RICScore. Our evaluation of 15 advanced open-source and closed-source VLMs identifies instance localization as a major bottleneck for these models. LocateAnything achieves the highest RICScore of 31.68, but scores lower on spatial relation captioning than other task-fine-tuned open-source VLMs. Code and dataset are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: RICapBench is a dataset and benchmark that unifies instance localisation and fine-grained captioning for remote sensing VLMs, with 245,466 instance annotations and 498,005 spatial relation tuples. It finds instance localisation to be the main bottleneck, with LocateAnything achieving the highest RICScore of 31.68.
AI.motivation: VLMs struggle with object scale, geospatial relations and limited detail in remote sensing imagery, and existing benchmarks do not assess end-to-end localisation and captioning without target-specific textual cues.
AI.method: Each annotation pairs an oriented bounding box with a natural-language description of the object's visible attributes and spatial relations. The benchmark spans general, UAV and dense small-object scenes. The authors propose a remote sensing spatial relation parser and the RelCap-F1 metric, combined with localisation and attribute metrics into the composite RICScore.
AI.result: Of 15 open-source and closed-source VLMs evaluated, LocateAnything achieves the highest RICScore of 31.68 but scores lower on spatial relation captioning than some task-fine-tuned open-source VLMs. Instance localisation is identified as a major bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: Localisation is the main limitation for current VLMs on fine-grained remote sensing captioning, and the benchmark makes this measurable.

title: VBot Exo2Ego Policy: Lightweight Data Collection and Exocentric-to-Egocentric Video Generation
summary: We present VBot Exo2Ego Policy, a video generation model that turns third-person videos into first-person observations of a selected actor, offering a practical way to expand first-person operation data from abundant real-world footage. To support this goal, we introduce a lightweight data collection pipeline and mobile app that support first-person recording, third-person recording, and synchronized capture of both views. This setup combines accessible single-view collection with paired RGB and camera geometry for learning cross-view correspondence. Building on a pretrained video diffusion transformer, our model incorporates geometric guidance and auxiliary supervision from semantic masks and hand keypoints to facilitate optimization and improve the fidelity of hand-object interactions. Camera geometry is injected stochastically during training and gradually removed, allowing inference without target-camera calibration. To accommodate the diversity of Internet videos, we combine source-video perception and reasoning, optional actor references, and multi-shot adaptation to identify the intended actor and follow an operation across camera cuts. The collection system and generation model provide a foundation for expanding first-person operation data across tasks, scenes, and participants.

AI.tldr: VBot Exo2Ego Policy is a video diffusion model that turns third-person videos into first-person views of a chosen actor, supported by a lightweight mobile data-collection app that records paired first- and third-person views. It injects camera geometry during training, removes it gradually, and does not need target-camera calibration at inference.
AI.motivation: First-person operation data is scarce, while third-person footage is abundant. The aim is to expand first-person data from real-world footage with accessible collection.
AI.method: The model builds on a pretrained video diffusion transformer and adds geometric guidance and auxiliary supervision from semantic masks and hand keypoints to improve hand-object interactions. Camera geometry is injected stochastically during training and gradually removed. Source-video perception and reasoning, optional actor references and multi-shot adaptation identify the intended actor across camera cuts.
AI.result: The abstract describes the model and data pipeline but gives no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The collection system and generation model provide a foundation for expanding first-person operation data across tasks, scenes and participants.

title: Model Distribution-Aware Multimodal Dataset Distillation
summary: Multimodal dataset distillation (MDD) aims to reduce the cost of vision-language pre-training by synthesizing compact image-text datasets. Although recent feature-matching methods have improved distillation efficiency, synthetic data may become specialized to the model representations encountered during optimization, limiting generalization to unseen model states. We propose Model Distribution-Aware Multimodal Dataset Distillation (MDA-DD), which leverages supervision from a dynamic staggered queue of models at different training stages. We further introduce asymmetric dual projection for complementary alignment in visual and linguistic spaces and an uncentered second-order moment objective that retains mean-related cross-modal information. Experiments on Flickr30K and MS-COCO demonstrate consistent retrieval improvements over existing methods across synthetic-data budgets. With only 100 synthetic pairs, MDA-DD improves IR@1 and TR@1 on Flickr30K by 12.9 and 18.2 percentage points, respectively, over the strongest baseline at the same budget, outperforming all compared methods using 500 pairs on both datasets across all six retrieval metrics.

AI.tldr: MDA-DD is a multimodal dataset distillation method that supervises synthetic image-text pairs with a dynamic staggered queue of models at different training stages, improving retrieval. With 100 synthetic pairs it improves Flickr30K IR@1 and TR@1 by 12.9 and 18.2 points over the strongest baseline at the same budget.
AI.motivation: Feature-matching distillation can specialise synthetic data to the model states seen during optimisation, which limits generalisation to unseen model states.
AI.method: MDA-DD uses supervision from a dynamic staggered queue of models at different training stages. It adds asymmetric dual projection for complementary alignment in visual and linguistic spaces, and an uncentred second-order moment objective that keeps mean-related cross-modal information.
AI.result: On Flickr30K and MS-COCO, retrieval improves consistently over existing methods across synthetic-data budgets. With 100 synthetic pairs, IR@1 and TR@1 on Flickr30K rise by 12.9 and 18.2 points over the strongest baseline at the same budget, outperforming all compared methods using 500 pairs on all six retrieval metrics.
AI.conclusion: Distilling against a distribution of training states rather than a single trajectory yields more general synthetic multimodal datasets, which is most valuable at very small budgets.

title: PhysCapBench: A Cross-Domain Benchmark for Physically Grounded Video Captioning
summary: Physical AI aims to learn transferable physical knowledge from real-world experience to understand, predict, and act in the physical world. Internet videos and embodied demonstrations provide complementary observations of motion, interaction, and state evolution. A foundational data challenge is to measure and preserve this physical information as training supervision. In video-language pretraining, captions express observed processes in language, yet a semantically correct description can omit the interactions and transitions that define those processes. Rich physical experience in video does not automatically translate into sufficient language supervision. This gap calls for a yardstick to assess annotation quality, compare captioning strategies, and guide training-data refinement. Motivated by our data construction for world-model pretraining, we introduce PhysCapBench, to our knowledge the first unified physical-caption benchmark spanning all three domains: third-person scenes, egocentric manipulation, and handheld-gripper demonstrations. It provides human-verified annotations for 1,500 video sequences and evaluates accuracy and coverage through seven physical dimensions. We examine downstream utility through video reconstruction and manipulation-policy fine-tuning. Physical captions reduce reconstruction LPIPS by 8.6-9.5% on third-person videos and 26.9-30.9% on egocentric videos relative to metadata captions. Training-instruction enrichment improves both PhysCapBench scores and policy success, including a 7.5-percentage-point gain for pi0.5 on a RoboTwin 2.0 subtask. PhysCapBench makes the physical content of language supervision inspectable and comparable, providing a cross-domain basis for its evaluation and improvement.

AI.tldr: PhysCapBench is a cross-domain benchmark of human-verified physical captions for 1,500 videos spanning third-person scenes, egocentric manipulation and handheld-gripper demonstrations, scored on seven physical dimensions. Physical captions reduce reconstruction LPIPS relative to metadata captions, and enrichment improves policy success.
AI.motivation: Captions can be semantically correct yet omit the interactions and transitions that define physical processes, so rich physical experience in video does not automatically become language supervision. A yardstick is needed to assess annotation quality.
AI.method: The benchmark provides human-verified annotations for 1,500 video sequences across three domains and evaluates accuracy and coverage through seven physical dimensions. Downstream utility is tested through video reconstruction and manipulation-policy fine-tuning.
AI.result: Physical captions reduce reconstruction LPIPS by 8.6 to 9.5% on third-person videos and 26.9 to 30.9% on egocentric videos relative to metadata captions. Training-instruction enrichment improves PhysCapBench scores and policy success, including a 7.5-point gain for pi0.5 on a RoboTwin 2.0 subtask.
AI.conclusion: PhysCapBench makes the physical content of language supervision inspectable and comparable across domains, supporting better captioning and training-data refinement.

title: DesignTaste: Benchmarking AI-Generator Visual Design Against Award-Wining Works
comment: 31 pages, 12 figures, including appendices. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Text-to-image benchmarks commonly assess text-image alignment or overall preference. Whether models can produce good designs when a brief leaves the appearance open remains less well understood. We introduce DesignTaste, a visual design benchmark that compares generated images with award-winning works. From these works and their publicly available context, we derive 403 design briefs: 100 poster tasks from 100 Beste Plakate 2025 and 303 tasks spanning 20 categories from ADC 2026. Six leading commercial text-to-image models each generate an image from the same brief. A single model judge scores each output and the corresponding award-winning work independently on five evaluation dimensions. On each dataset, only ArtArk achieves a higher mean overall score than the award-winning works. All six models score lower in Creative Originality on both datasets. These results show that producing finished, visually appealing images does not imply that a model can develop good design solutions.

AI.tldr: DesignTaste benchmarks text-to-image models against award-winning designs, using 403 briefs derived from Beste Plakate 2025 and ADC 2026. Only one of six commercial models, ArtArk, beats the award-winning works on mean overall score, and all six score lower on Creative Originality.
AI.motivation: Text-to-image benchmarks assess alignment or overall preference, but not whether models produce good designs when a brief leaves the appearance open.
AI.method: The authors derive 403 design briefs from award-winning works and their public context: 100 poster tasks from Beste Plakate 2025 and 303 tasks across 20 categories from ADC 2026. Six commercial text-to-image models generate an image per brief. A single model judge scores each output and the award-winning work independently on five dimensions.
AI.result: On each dataset, only ArtArk achieves a higher mean overall score than the award-winning works. All six models score lower in Creative Originality on both datasets.
AI.conclusion: Producing finished, visually appealing images does not mean a model can develop good design solutions, and creative originality remains a clear gap.

title: HIFC-IQA: Train-Free Cross-Domain Image Quality Assessment via Dual-Process Cognition
summary: The gap between controlled synthetic distortions and complex real-world degradations introduces a critical domain shift challenge for No-Reference Image Quality Assessment. Although Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) approaches attempt to address this issue, they remain constrained by substantial retraining overhead and cumulative error propagation inherent in iterative pseudo-labeling. Inspired by the dual-process theory of human cognition for remarkable generalization ability, we propose Hierarchical Intuitive and Fuzzy Consensus (HIFC), a completely train-free Cross-Domain IQA framework. HIFC employs asymmetric perceptual decomposition to disentangle semantic content from distortion-sensitive representations. The final quality score is fused through the synergy of two complementary branches: a memory consensus branch that retrieves a stable Fuzzy Quality Centroid from a synthetic reference gallery, and an intuitive branch that captures aesthetic polarization via zero-shot vision-language alignment. Extensive experiments show that HIFC achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks, attaining the highest average SRCC and PLCC among competing UDA methods. Most notably, in the challenging synthetic-to-authentic cross-domain setting, HIFC achieves a substantial performance margin over competing methods, demonstrating remarkable robustness and generalization.

AI.tldr: HIFC-IQA is a train-free cross-domain image quality assessment framework that combines a memory consensus branch, which retrieves a fuzzy quality centroid from a synthetic reference gallery, with a zero-shot vision-language intuitive branch. It reports the highest average SRCC and PLCC among UDA methods, with the largest margin in synthetic-to-authentic transfer.
AI.motivation: No-reference IQA suffers a domain shift between controlled synthetic distortions and real-world degradations. UDA methods need costly retraining and suffer error accumulation from iterative pseudo-labelling.
AI.method: Inspired by dual-process cognition, HIFC uses asymmetric perceptual decomposition to separate semantic content from distortion-sensitive representations. The final score fuses a memory consensus branch, which retrieves a Fuzzy Quality Centroid from a synthetic reference gallery, with an intuitive branch that captures aesthetic polarisation through zero-shot vision-language alignment.
AI.result: HIFC achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks, with the highest average SRCC and PLCC among competing UDA methods. In the synthetic-to-authentic setting it shows a substantial margin over competing methods. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: A train-free, dual-branch design can generalise across domains without retraining or pseudo-label drift.

title: Can an LVLM Perceive Event Boundaries Like a Human?
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) reason effectively about video content, but whether they perceive its event boundaries in a manner consistent with humans remains unclear. We first investigate this through Generic Event Boundary Detection (GEBD), which identifies event boundaries naturally perceived by humans in continuous video, without relying on predefined event categories. On Kinetics-GEBD dataset, LVLMs miss many boundaries when predicting directly from frames, but effectively refine candidates proposed by an unsupervised discovery method, achieving state-of-the-art unsupervised GEBD performance. We extend this discovery-refinement approach to hour-long egocentric video, where boundary discovery requires a broader semantic scale and whole-video LVLM refinement becomes impractical. We address these challenges through coarse-to-fine temporal discovery and localized LVLM accept/reject judgments. Human evaluation shows that the LVLM's agreement with group consensus falls within the range observed among human annotators, with disagreements concentrated on low-consensus cases. Using this pipeline, we construct EgoBoundary, a benchmark for event boundary detection in hour-scale egocentric video. Representative supervised and unsupervised methods degrade substantially on EgoBoundary, highlighting the challenge of long-horizon event boundary detection.

title: PiLLVD: A Real-World Low-Light Video Dataset for Dynamic Scenes Captured with Off-the-Shelf Cameras
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables. Dataset available on Zenodo: this https URL
summary: Low-light image and video enhancement has received increasing attention in recent years. However, most existing enhancement methods are developed and evaluated on still images, while progress in low-light video enhancement remains limited by the lack of real-world paired video datasets. Acquiring paired low-light and normal-light video sequences is challenging because it requires spatially and temporally aligned captures while avoiding motion blur, exposure mismatch, and correspondence errors in dynamic scenes. To address this gap, we introduce PiLLVD, the Pi-based Low-Light Video Dataset, a paired low-light video dataset captured using an accessible Raspberry Pi-based multi-camera system with off-the-shelf cameras. PiLLVD provides paired low-light and aligned normal-light reference sequences for dynamic indoor and outdoor scenes, including diverse human and object motion under varying illumination conditions. Unlike existing datasets that are often image-based, static, synthetic, or limited to simple motion patterns, PiLLVD focuses on motion-rich scenes where frame-to-frame stability and motion-related artefacts are important for evaluation. In addition to presenting the dataset and acquisition pipeline, we benchmark representative pre-trained low-light video enhancement methods on PiLLVD under a zero-shot setting. The results show that existing methods do not generalise uniformly across the proposed sequences, highlighting the challenges posed by the proposed dataset and its value for both benchmarking existing methods and supporting the development of future low-light video enhancement algorithms.
